items.cleanReaderHtml:
Model and ballet dancer Sheena Liam brings her understanding of poise, elegance, and graceful bodily movements to a more fixed medium. For the past several years, the artist has been stitching tender portraits of women with long, three-dimensional braids that cascade off the fabric. Occasionally, a single loose thread appears to have slipped out of its plait as it drifts across a protagonist’s cheek.

Liam’s latest works are on view this month in her solo exhibition, The Unbearable Lightness. Several pieces feature figures sporting the same striped bodysuit with an open back, and the methodical pattern on the garment evokes both a sense of precision and rhythm depicted in the scenes. Dancers grasp hands in a circle, clutch each other at the waist, and quietly stretch in solitude, their movements steady and self-determined.

Created across the last eight years, this body of work extends Liam’s interest in women’s labor and how the slow, careful process of stitching can also be an act of defiance in an increasingly digital, fast-paced world. Each piece begins with an underlying sketch that the artist then covers in thread and typically finishes with sleek braids and quick snips of the remaining loose ends.

The Unbearable Lightness opens today at Item Gallery in Paris and runs through December 19. Follow Liam’s latest on Instagram.

items.title: Nine-Pound Eagles Seem to Be Hunting 60-Pound Baboons in Africa—Hinting the Predators May Have Gone After Our Ancestors, Too
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: In northeastern Chad, researchers found evidence of Verreaux's eagles attacking full-grown olive baboons weighing as much as a small human. The findings suggest early hominins had to watch out for ambushes from the sky, which may have shaped their evolution

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Smart News
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Sarah Kuta
An illustration of a large bird approaching a baboon, next to an image of a baboon skull with an eagle claw

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Eagles are formidable aerial predators capable of taking down animals much larger than themselves, including primates. But scientists have long believed that eagles tend to go after smaller primates, generally weighing less than 30 pounds.

New research suggests otherwise. Scientists have found evidence of Verreaux’s eagles hunting full-grown olive baboons weighing nearly 60 pounds, which they describe in a study published November 18 in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology .

The findings add to scientists’ understanding of predator-prey relationships. But they also raise the intriguing new possibility that eagle attacks might have influenced human evolution. Some of our ancestors, such as Australopithecus afarensis , weighed about as much as modern baboons, so it’s plausible that eagles went after them, too, millions of years ago. The threat of these attacks, researchers posit, might have affected how early humans communicated and cooperated with one another.

In February and March 2025, primatologists went looking for olive baboons on the Ennedi Plateau , a remote area in northeastern Chad filled with sandstone cliffs, gorges and rock formations. They were hoping to collect genetic samples so they could chart the history of the baboons’ movement across Africa.

But the focus of their expedition took an unexpected turn when they stumbled upon an olive baboon skull with a distinctive hole at the back of one of the eye sockets—clear evidence that a razor-sharp eagle talon had speared the primate’s head. The researchers had noticed Verreaux’s eagles soaring overhead, but it hadn’t occurred to them that the birds might be going after the baboons.

During that initial trip, they recovered the remains of nine olive baboons, including eight adult males. Two of the skulls had talon-shaped puncture marks, while one shoulder blade was covered in what appeared to be talon scratch marks. In June 2026, they found another skull and partial skeleton, which also showed signs of eagle predation.

The study authors can’t definitively rule out scavenging. But “the severity of punctures is suggestive of lethal interactions through a killing grip,” they write in the paper.

Further supporting the idea that Verreaux’s eagles were actively hunting the baboons, not just scavenging their remains, the scientists noted how groups of baboons responded whenever the birds got close, based on previously published observations. As soon as Verreaux’s eagles came into view, the primates started warning each other with alarm calls and taking cover. The baboons didn’t behave this way when other big birds of prey were nearby, suggesting they viewed the Verreaux’s eagles—which typically max out at about nine pounds—as legitimate threats.

“At first, the idea of eagles hunting adult male baboons seemed to exist on the thin edge of possibility, until it didn’t,” study co-author Nathaniel Dominy , a primatologist at Dartmouth College, says in a statement . “Our skepticism slowly gave way to acceptance. The evidence was convincing.”

The scientists estimate that, when they were alive, the baboons whose remains they initially discovered weighed approximately 49 pounds on average. But the one found in 2026 appears to have been much heavier, possibly weighing as much as 58 pounds. That’s well within the range of early hominin species: “ Lucy ,” the famous A. afarensis individual who lived in what is now Ethiopia roughly 3.2 million years ago, is believed to have weighed about 62 pounds.

The only known case of an eagle hunting and killing an ancient hominin is the Taung Child , reports Live Science . The A. africanus individual is estimated to have been about 3 at death, and their skull contains puncture marks at the bottom of the eye sockets.

Scientists know that our ancestors were vulnerable to attacks from ground-based predators like crocodiles and hyenas. But the new findings suggest they might also have needed to be on alert for ambushes from the sky.

That could have affected their behavior. Modern primates that live in areas with predatory eagles tend to move around in large groups made up of various primate species. “That means extra competition for the food—but the benefits of the added protection seem to be worth the cost,” lead author Catherine Hobaiter , a primatologist at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland, tells Live Science ’s Owen Jarus.

Perhaps our ancestors deployed a similar strategy, learning to cooperate, rather than compete, with other hominin and primate species because they discovered there’s safety in numbers. They might also have evolved other adaptations in response to potential eagle attacks, such as calling out to warn others or living in places where they could easily hide.

items.author: Regan Penaluna
items.summary: A new chapter in evolutionary biology argues that animals’ bright colors and patterns are about more than just sex The post What Do Peahens Really Want? appeared first on Nautilus .

items.cleanReaderHtml:
A new chapter in evolutionary biology argues that animals’ bright colors and patterns are about more than just sex

First of all, there was the trick of staying submerged long enough to hear him. My 3-millimeter wetsuit was made of neoprene, a rubber infused with tiny gas bubbles, and I felt as buoyant as a cork. I was off the coast of Mo’orea, a small island in French Polynesia, floating on the deep cerulean-blue sea.

I could just make him out in the distance: the faint white outline of pectoral fins and underbelly, a ghostly silhouette of a male humpback whale suspended vertically, nose pointing down to the ocean floor. He was a giant school bus of a creature dwarfed only by the ocean itself, yet whose song commanded the great expanse. His plaintive chant—ascending high notes interrupted with bass staccatos that caused my flippers to vibrate—was amplified by the walls of the barrier reef. I was getting cold, but the pleasure of his song overpowered my numbing limbs. I wanted to keep myself in the presence of beauty for just a moment longer.

This story is from “The Hot Issue,” the latest from Nautilus . To get it in print, join by Nov 30 .

Beauty. Did other whales off the coast of Mo’orea hear beauty in the song? Do other animals sense beauty?

None other than Charles Darwin thought so. He believed animals got pleasure from admiring shapes, colors, patterns, and sounds. On visits to the Zoological Gardens in London, he enjoyed the peacocks’ decorated, iridescent plumes, and imagined that the peahens admired the peacock’s tail “as much as we do.” Birds weren’t the only nonhuman aesthetes. Darwin thought spiders had an eye for beauty, too. He mused that since we evolved from a common ancestor, it’s possible that much more life on Earth could have a “taste for the beautiful.”

Yet the biological processes for how this might work remained a mystery to him. In On the Origin of Species , published in 1859, Darwin circled the riddle of how life evolved from a common ancestor through natural selection, and later, in The Descent of Man , he was concerned with the nature of animals’ sense of beauty. The first was solved a century later with the discovery of genetic inheritance through DNA. The second riddle is still an open question.

Most scientists after Darwin—biologists especially—dropped the question entirely. Victorians didn’t like the idea that the appreciation of beauty, often considered evidence of the soul, could be shared with beasts. There was also growing consensus among scientists that nonhuman animal traits and behaviors could be explained through the evolutionary goals of sex, food, and shelter alone. Even now it’s met with suspicion. Beauty, the assumption goes, is in the eye of the beholder, who can only be human.

But modern evolutionary biologists have gathered evidence that animals from baboons to birds, honeybees to fish, might have a sense of beauty. As squishy as that might sound, a large body of research in psychology, neurobiology, and computational neuroscience treats beauty as an empirical phenomenon that can be defined and tested. Although most of this research focuses on humans, scientists believe there are strong parallels that can be drawn to nonhuman animals.

Tamra Mendelson, a professor of evolutionary biology and behavioral ecology at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, is a leader in the field. She’s heard all the criticisms of her work being anthropomorphic. One day, after she gave a talk proposing that nonhuman animals share brain processes with us that correlate with experiencing beauty, a colleague walked up to her and said, “You know, this is all really great but just drop the beauty part.”

“I’m not going to drop it,” Mendelson said to me recently with a warm laugh. “Beauty is real. It’s a real experience. You have it. He has it. We’re all animals, and we have it.”

In what ways, though, do animals sense beauty? What role does it play in mating, in adaptation and evolution? Mendelson and her colleagues answer those questions and boldly propose that beauty is its “own self-sufficient source of pleasure,” as they write in a 2025 paper, “On the biological basis of beauty.” We’re not the only ones on this planet to enjoy something simply for its beauty. Animals too might experience beauty for beauty’s sake.

Mendelson didn’t study beauty at the outset of her scientific career. She was struck by it instead. While a graduate student at Duke University, she had a stint between 1993 and 1994 studying lemurs at the Duke Lemur Center, where she found herself chasing after the primates in the cold to record whether the dominant female gets to be the warmest by being in the middle of the huddle.

Her luck changed when a mentor handed her a bunch of papers on darters, a fish species native to North America found in the shallows of streams and lakes. Mendelson knew she’d found her ideal candidate. Darters could be studied in a laboratory aquarium that recreates their natural habitat, and she could watch them while seated with a cup of coffee. That wasn’t the only perk. It was also their looks. “I can’t stand it, they’re so beautiful,” she said.

items.title: Network Researchers Nail Down Theory of ‘Perfect Resilience’
items.author: Ben Brubaker
items.summary: When links in a communication network go down, messages can get routed in a loop. Computer scientists now know that four simple network structures are to blame. The post Network Researchers Nail Down Theory of ‘Perfect Resilience’ first appeared on Quanta Magazine

One evening in the fall of 1969, a team of researchers sent a historic message from a computer in Los Angeles to one in Menlo Park, California. Or rather, they sent part of the message: the “L” and “O” in “LOGIN.” The first transmission over the first link in Arpanet, the prototype for the modern internet, lasted all of two characters before the network crashed.

Computer networks have grown much more reliable since that first test nearly 60 years ago. But we also demand a lot more of them. When you watch a movie online, the video data gets divided into a series of tiny “packets” that hop between way stations called routers on their way to your computer. Links between routers sometimes fail. One reason our videos aren’t constantly glitching out is that each router has a thorough contingency plan — a set of rules for redirecting packets in case a link goes down.

If a large outage cuts off every path between two points, there’s no way a packet can get through. But ideally, a network would be able to withstand any pattern of link failures short of this worst-case scenario. Researchers call this property “perfect resilience.” For over a decade, computer scientists have sought to understand what kinds of networks can be made perfectly resilient under realistic conditions.

Now, in a paper that was presented at the Symposium on Theory of Computing in June 2026, two researchers have settled the question with a comprehensive proof. They showed that there are exactly four minimal network structures that can thwart perfect resilience. In networks that lack these structures, you can always concoct rules that will reliably deliver packets from any source to any destination, regardless of which links fail.

“It’s a very elegant contribution,” said Michael Schapira , a computer scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem who was not involved in the result. “It’s pretty rare that you get a complete understanding of something.”

Imagine you have a network of routers in which each device can direct data packets bound for any other point in the network. You can then ask yourself: What instructions should the routers follow?

The first router for Arpanet, the predecessor of the internet.

One simple approach would be to map out the shortest path between every pair of points in the network, and then give each router a copy of the map. If the network ever changes — if even a single link fails — start over and do it again.

In principle, this strategy will ensure that every packet reaches its destination. In practice, it’s far too slow. Calculating shortest paths is inherently a “global” problem — it requires knowledge of the entire network. In a real-world network, that calculation might take up to a few seconds. But each router has to act fast, in a fraction of a millisecond or less. That means routers must direct packets using only locally accessible information, such as the status of links to their immediate neighbors.

This restriction makes the problem of perfect resilience much more complicated. Without any global coordination between routers, packets might get trapped in loops.

In a 2012 paper, Schapira and five other researchers formally defined perfect resilience and devised a mathematical model to study when it’s achievable. They assumed that routing rules must have a simple form. A router can decide in which direction to send each new packet using only three factors: the packet’s destination, the link it arrived on, and which neighboring links have failed. The rules can’t depend on the path that a packet has taken so far, since routers don’t have access to this information.

With these assumptions, the researchers aimed to capture “something very close to how networks actually operate,” said Brighten Godfrey , a computer scientist at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign who co-authored the 2012 paper.

In 2020, Stefan Schmid and his colleagues proved a partial result about the reliability of communication networks.

items.title: Teeth Discovered in Two Chinese Caves Are Rewriting the Story of Homo Erectus, an Ancient Human Ancestor That May Have Been More Capable Than We Thought
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: One new study suggests that the species persisted in mainland Asia for 216,000 years longer than previously thought. Another says Homo erectus was capable of living in a tropical rainforest, a discovery that turns a common extinction theory "on its head," according to one researcher

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Smart News
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Sarah Kuta
A graphic showing different teeth

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Homo erectus was thought to have disappeared from mainland Asia roughly 400,000 years ago. But newly discovered fossils suggest that the species survived there for much longer, possibly living in southern China as recently as 184,000 years ago. The fossils also show for the first time that H. erectus was capable of living in a tropical rainforest environment.

The findings, described in two new papers published in the journal Nature , are based on recent analyses of H. erectus teeth. One paper finds that H. erectus persisted on mainland Asia for up to 216,000 years longer than previously thought, while the other indicates that the species was even more ecologically flexible than scientists assumed.

Scientists think H. erectus arose in Africa about 1.89 million years ago. It’s believed to be the first hominin species to have spread beyond the continent, with populations reaching what is now Georgia, on the border between Europe and Asia, by about 1.8 million years ago. The species continued spreading east into what is now China, eventually reaching the Indonesian island of Java.

Eugène Dubois , a Dutch anatomist and geologist, made the first discovery of an H. erectus fossil, in the early 1890s. He unearthed a skullcap and femur belonging to the so-called Java Man on the eponymous island.

H. erectus had a more modern, humanlike body than earlier hominins, with long legs and short arms suited to walking and running over long distances. The species made increasingly sophisticated stone tools, probably used fire , and hunted and butchered big game .

Scientists were excavating two limestone caves, located about nine miles apart in China’s Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region , when they stumbled upon nine hominin teeth. They used computed tomography (CT) scanning and physical examinations to investigate the teeth, ultimately determining that eight belonged to H. erectus . The identity of the ninth tooth, however, remains unknown.

Researchers also recovered ancient protein from five of the teeth, including the mystery tooth. In the four H. erectus teeth, they found a version of a protein called ameloblastin that had only previously been seen in older Asian H. erectus fossils.

The mystery tooth also contained ameloblastin, however, it didn’t match any known hominin. For now, that tooth remains unidentified, but Frido Welker , a molecular anthropologist at the University of Copenhagen who co-authored one of the studies, tells Scientific American ’s Jacek Krywko that he thinks Denisovans , hominins who lived across Asia from roughly 400,000 to about 30,000 years ago, “would be the first option to consider.” He suspects the two species overlapped in what is now southern China, but cautioned that scientists will need to conduct additional research to definitively identify the tooth.

The researchers used numerous methods to date the H. erectus teeth, deducing that they’re likely between 324,000 and 184,000 years old. At that time, the region seems to have been a tropical rainforest—a new and surprising ecosystem for H. erectus.

“Rainforests were thought to be a frontier that only modern humans could survive and cross,” Ben Marwick , an archaeologist at the University of Washington who was not involved with the new research, tells National Geographic ’s Christina Larson. “But now it seems this idea of Homo sapiens exceptionalism may not be the true story.”

Additional analyses of the teeth revealed that these H. erectus individuals traveled long distances, possibly coming to southern China from as far away as what is now northern Vietnam, some 155 miles away. Making that kind of journey would have required “a sophisticated understanding of the surrounding terrain, including regional landscape features and river networks that change with the seasons,” Ben Utting , an archaeologist at the University of Connecticut who was not involved with the new studies, tells CNN ’s Katie Hunt.

Together, the findings add to the growing picture of the species’ behavioral and ecological flexibility, Karen Baab , a paleoanthropologist at Midwestern University who was not involved with the new work, tells New Scientist ’s Michael Marshall. “They seemed quite adaptable and flexible in general, because of the incredible range of niches they were occupying,” she adds.

That flexibility probably helped H. erectus persist for roughly 1.8 to 1.9 million years—six times longer than modern humans—making it the longest-surviving known species in the Homo genus.

However, scientists still don’t know why the species went extinct between 108,000 to 117,000 years ago. The leading theory is that H. erectus couldn’t adapt when rainforests started encroaching on their final home, the island of Java.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Camera traps are important devices for conservationists and photographers, providing a non-invasive way in which they can keep tabs on the behaviors and movements of wildlife over time. Occasionally, camera traps also help to identify a new species too.

Case in point: A camera trap embedded in the Alta Floresta region of the Amazon rainforest, toward the western edge of Brazil, snapped a photo of a new howler monkey species, Alouatta matogrossensis , not long after the species was first described in a study in Communications Biology .

Read more: “ Qatari Sand Cats Caught on Camera for the First Time ”

Conservationists set up the trap on the end of a rope bridge installed to keep forested areas connected for tree-dwelling animals. Such bridges enable them to safely cross roads and prevent populations from declining through isolation. “We were all amazed that we were providing safe crossing opportunities for a new monkey species,” Fernanda Abra, a road ecologist who leads Projecto Reconecta , told National Geographic .

As is often the case when a new species is discovered, this type of howler monkey is under threat from several environmental pressures. If it wasn’t, experts likely would have come across it earlier.

In fact, A. matogrossensis has been hiding in plain sight. Previously, researchers had filed it away as being a more common Purus red howler ( Alouatta puruensis ). The fresh analysis of its genetic and physical characteristics revealed the distinction. The team behind the new study thinks A. matogrossensis may have been around for some 500,000 years, contained by rivers on one side of their natural habitat, and by a tropical savanna on the other.

According to study author Jean Boubli , from the University of Salford in the U.K., this patch of ecosystem is “where the forest is at its worst shape in the whole of Brazil.” Deforestation related to agriculture and urbanization has left smaller and smaller areas for these animals to live, even without considering the threat from road vehicle collisions.

With new rope bridges and camera traps—as well as a better understanding of the species that live in this part of the world—conservationists now have a better chance of helping the howler monkey population to grow—and discovering even more species before it’s too late.

David Nield has written about science and technology for more than 20 years. His work has appeared in a wide range of publications, including Wired, Popular Science, The Guardian , and Gizmodo .

items.cleanReaderHtml:
For millennia, roses have been capturing the admiration of humans, who have shown their appreciation for the flower in myriad ways. Poems, songs, nursery rhymes and more have praised the plant. Among some European nobles, roses and rose water were once so precious that they were considered legal tender. Vincent van Gogh has immortalized them on canvas.

President Ronald Reagan named it America’s national flower in 1986. “We hold the rose dear as the symbol of life and love and devotion, of beauty and eternity,” Regan wrote in his official proclamation.

Likewise, these Smithsonian Magazine Photo Contest entrants considered the flower worthy of their artistic attention. Take a look.

items.title: Georgia O'Keeffe Is Famous for Painting Flowers and Deserts. Why Have We Forgotten Her Obsession With American Architecture?

items.summary: Featuring nearly 40 artworks, a new exhibition at the Detroit Institute of Arts spotlights the artist's mesmerizing portrayals of the built environment, from rural farmhouses to city skyscrapers

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Georgia O’Keeffe started visiting New Mexico in 1929, immersing herself in the state’s austere desert landscapes for months at a time. She captured her surroundings in hundreds of paintings, which are now some of her best-known works.

But while she found the scenery striking, nature was only part of the American Southwest’s aesthetic appeal. In the 1930s, the artist stumbled across an abandoned house in Abiquiú , which she later purchased. O’Keeffe was particularly fascinated by a large wooden door leading to the central patio, a feature she painted at least 20 times .

“I bought the place because it had that door in the patio, the one I’ve painted so often,” she said in a 1962 interview . “I’m always trying to paint that door—I never quite get it. It’s a curse—the way I feel I must continually go on with that door.”

O’Keeffe is considered one of America’s greatest artists , and general audiences are familiar with her desert landscapes and large-scale flower portraits. But now, an exhibition at the Detroit Institute of Arts spotlights a lesser-known part of her oeuvre: her enduring fascination with the built environment.

“This is the first exhibit that takes a comprehensive view of architecture as a lifelong fascination for O’Keeffe,” Ben Colman , the exhibition’s curator, tells the New York Times ’ Leslie Wayne. “Barns and fields and buildings are not the O’Keeffe that people think about. It’s a bit of a surprise.”

“ Georgia O’Keeffe: Architecture ” features nearly 40 works created between the 1920s and 1960s. The artist’s paintings are grouped into three sections, each exploring a central setting from her life: rural barns and farmhouses, New York City skyscrapers, and New Mexico homes.

Stables , a painting of a white barn that the artist noticed during a 1932 road trip through Quebec, served as the inspiration for the exhibition. It’s the only O’Keeffe in the Detroit Institute of Arts’ collections. When Colman joined the institute in 2015, he was fascinated by its simple geometric shapes and large blocks of color. He found himself thinking about it often.

“I had such a strong pull to this picture and wanted to know more,” Colman says in an interview posted on the institute’s website. “In asking questions about Stables , I started to sketch out a broader story about O’Keeffe’s life and her engagement with architecture across her career. What began as a set of questions about the summer of 1932 turned into a larger story about the role architecture played as a recurring source of inspiration throughout the artist’s life.”

Stables is on display in the exhibition’s first section, which reflects O’Keeffe’s childhood on a Wisconsin dairy farm, as well as her sojourns to Lake George in upstate New York with her husband, photographer Alfred Stieglitz .

Another highlight of this section is My Shanty, Lake George (1922). Colman describes it as “a challenge to her critics,” who struggled to evaluate O’Keeffe’s art without considering her gender.

“One day as I looked at the brown burned wood of the Shanty, I thought, ‘I can paint one of those dismal-colored paintings like the men. I think just for fun I will try—all low-toned and dreary,’” O’Keeffe wrote in her 1976 autobiography . When My Shanty, Lake George went on display, “the men seemed to approve of it,” she added. “They seemed to think that maybe I was beginning to paint.”

The second section showcases paintings of high-rises in New York City , where the artist lived for three decades. One of the pieces on view is Brooklyn Bridge (1949), the final city artwork that O’Keeffe created before moving away. She painted it from the perspective of someone passing through the bridge’s famous archways.

“It captures a view that you only see when you’re crossing the river, when you’re in the midst of making a change yourself,” Colman says. “The artist created this painting the year that she relocated her life and home to New Mexico permanently.”

The final section displays O’Keeffe’s paintings of New Mexico, where she lived until her death at age 98 in 1986. These paintings capture the region’s unique adobe architecture—including ten depictions of that inscrutable patio door.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Along the rugged volcanic coast of Iceland’s Reykjanes Peninsula, Vilhelm Gunnarsson captures striking storm surf amid natural contrasts. Dark rocks and beaches send foamy waves into high definition, highlighting the forces that physically shape the artist’s home country. Using black-and-white, an approach inspired by fellow artist Ragnar Axelsson, Gunnarsson emphasizes profound tonal shifts and incredible vistas.

Doubling as a press photographer and a member of a local rescue team, Gunnarsson is accustomed to working in a range of conditions. He captured these images during or just after a storm, when the waves are at their highest. Once you see an otherworldly face emerging from one of the crests, which the photographer describes as a ghost, you won’t be able to unsee it. Explore a larger archive on Instagram.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
recently completed a Master of Divinity postgraduate degree at Harvard Divinity School, focusing on comparative religion and sacred landscapes. She is originally from Bangor, Maine.

In October 1948, in Country Kerry, Ireland, Seán Ó Muircheartaigh met with Seosamh Ó Dálaigh to tell him about the woman who came from the sea. She had appeared, said Ó Muircheartaigh, one night on the magharees, those bright spits of sand that occasionally pop up amid the rain-lashed rocks of the Dingle peninsula. Alone on the beach, she settled herself on a rock and began combing her hair.

Also on the beach was a farmer, who – much to the surprise of the woman herself – would by daybreak become her husband. He’d come to gather seaweed, seeing her before she saw him. Beautiful as she was, the woman was also strange: the creature he saw stagger onto that Dingle beach was not a woman at all. It was a seal.

By the time Ó Muircheartaigh told Ó Dálaigh about the seal woman, he was already 80. He had been born in the apocalyptic aftermath of the Great Hunger that divested as much as a third of Ireland’s population to death or migration, and he had survived two great wars. Most of the disappeared were – like Ó Muircheartaigh himself – small farmers and native Irish, or Gaeilge, speakers. The famine had been not just a physical genocide: it had been a linguistic and cultural one, too.

Both Ó Muircheartaigh and Ó Dálaigh were veteran contributors to the Irish Folklore Commission: the former as a renowned storyteller; the latter, an equally renowned collector. The IFC is now the National Folklore Collection at University College Dublin ­– a behemoth of 3 million pages of texts and recordings. But in 1948, following eight centuries of colonialism, the loss of 99 per cent of the island’s forests, a staggering emigration , and the decline of the Irish language, the IFC was in a race against time and the fragility of memory. As it turned out, an awful lot of people had heard stories about seals that came to land as humans.

N owadays, these shapeshifters are known as ‘selkies’. Selkie is a Scots term that came into widespread use via a Joan Baez cover, ‘Silkie’ (1961), of a traditional Scottish folk song. Yet the phenomenon it describes – of creatures who shapeshift between human and seal forms by shedding a skin – appears consistently in folklore spanning the Celtic world and beyond, even as far as Sweden. Before Baez insinuated the term into international parlance, selkies were identified in Irish and English by a constellation of descriptors. In Irish, the most common is mhaighdean mhara , or ‘sea maiden’, referring to selkies and mermaids. Even in English, many storytellers use ‘mermaid’ for both the phocine and the piscine. Sometimes the two are differentiated with context (fish tails, seal skins), but what matters more than phenotyping is that the mermaid or selkie is neither quite human nor animal. What defines the selkie is transformation.

Much of the folklore retains the quality of the best gossip, hyper-local and yet vague. Storytellers name names, offer precise locations for key scenes in the story. And several admit something startling: that they themselves are the descendants of human-seal pairings.

After the farmer spotted the woman on the beach, Ó Muircheartaigh said, he saw something else. A sealskin cloak lay beside her: her ticket to transformation and a return to the sea. Then he made a choice that would ricochet throughout the generations, and leave the selkie with no option but to follow him home. He stole the selkie’s cloak and secreted it away, thus securing her for a bride. These rough beginnings aside, the couple produced a brood of children and went about the gruelling lives of any impoverished Irish fishing family. The only thing disrupting the fantasy of a normal human wife, acquired in normal human ways, was the webbing between the children’s toes. That, and the fact that the woman never smiled, but kept looking out towards the sea.

W hat does it mean if your grandmother was a seal? The folklore attests that marriages between humans and selkies were common enough to generate a host of human-selkie lineages – Conneely, Gallagher, Dowd, O’Kane, O’Shea, MacDuffie, McPhee, Flaherty, Glavin – whose members were predisposed towards webbed digits and an ineffable longing for the sea. (‘My mother was one of them O’Sheas,’ the railway worker Séamas MacMathghamhna confided to a folklore collector in 1949, after explaining the selkie lineage of the O’Sheas.) The Celtic studies scholar Gregory Darwin has identified nearly 50 family groups whose members carry selkie blood.

Now is a good time to have a seal in the family tree. As our planet hurtles through climate catastrophe, everyone from environmental activists and TikTok influencers to academics and New Age pilgrims is turning towards animals-as-family rhetoric. Such gusto stems from a cultural exhaustion with extractionism and with narratives of domination and human exceptionalism that have dogged the culture and geopolitics of the Global North since the 19th century. Yet the naivety with which the zeitgeist tends to approach an expanded view of interspecies kinship presents its own problems. For one, it doesn’t quite ring true – and it is hard to fight for a worldview that you can’t see clearly. For another, if we reframe our relationship with the more-than-human around intimate familial connection, then we need ways of understanding what happens when that connection becomes fraught.

The selkie story is one of family dysfunction par excellence. After all, the gutting truth at the centre of selkie families is that one’s origins lie in theft, violence, rape and unimaginable loss. The children of human-selkie pairings face a mottled inheritance, at best. Writing for The New York Times in 2008, Bryan Patrick Miller recounted how his great-great-great-grandfather’s kidnapping of a mhaighdean mhara cursed the family, causing the couple’s half-human children to flee across the Atlantic. Some coastal communities saw seals as fallen angels or the souls of drowned fishermen: mating with them was dubious to say the least.

Mottled or not, a selkie genealogy had to be reckoned with. Having a selkie in the family forced an acknowledgement of a mixed inheritance that was dark and disturbing, and in which successive generations continued to be implicated. Only by considering these uncomfortable reverberations of what it means to be family do we move closer to reimagining our relationships with the more-than-human world.

A woman who is sexually unsatisfied in her marriage may cry into the sea and receive a selkie who is an absolute dynamo in bed

Among folklorists, the trope of the selkie is generally known as the Seal Wife – a designation that speaks more to the gendered hold that the selkie story has on our imagination than to the actual folklore topos. The selkie’s allure is such that men will risk curses and commit theft and kidnapping to possess her, regardless of the certain tragedy that forced marriage augurs. Yet the selkies of folklore are not necessarily wives, women or even seals (note the mermaids, above). Male selkies occasionally make cameos as the kidnapped selkie wife’s jilted husband, father of her aquatic children, keening for her release from outside the human husband’s house. At other times, they appear as her brother, or as characters in the quotidian interactions between humans and their environment: they are accidentally killed, kidnapped as pets, steal fish, issue prophesies, plead and bargain, proffer advice and opinions.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Nothing in visual culture is neutral, least of all the color wheel itself. Scholar Richard Powell explores this deceptively simple truth in his new book, tackling the theoretical entanglement of race and pigment and how Black painters have used color over time. Trailblazing art historian Lowery Stokes Sims, formerly a curator at the Met Museum and director of the Studio Museum in Harlem, parses his richly layered essays today, linking the critical theory of Josef Albers and Darby English to the practices of artists like Jacob Lawrence and Alma Thomas. The book, Sims writes, shifted the way she’ll look at art moving forward.

Meanwhile, on the other end of the spectrum: News broke that a 1920 painting by Hilma af Klint sold for $12.7 million. Yes, the same Hilma af Klint who described herself less as an artist and more as a channel for a higher power, who followed the guidance of spirits that took physical form through her paintings. But hey, at least the painting’s owner has a new addition to their investment portfolio?

In reviews, Alina Cohen spends time with the poignant, impactful photographs by Laia Abril, who evokes the systems of patriarchy and sexual violence through the quietly haunting garments and objects in their wake. As the Cornell 7 case continues and convicted abusers sit in office, Abril’s photographs “reject both the invisibility of some crimes and the all-too-visible nature of others.” More, as always, below.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books

Richard Powell Unsettles Race and Color Theory

I was aware of the place of color theory in the practice of art and knew the names of important theorists, from Johann Wolfgang von Goethe to Johannes Itten to Josef Albers. But otherwise, I presumed artists’ palettes were the result of personal predilection, technical explorations (i.e., the opening up of brushstrokes and form in the 19th century and the introduction of a wall of color in the 20th century), or cultural orientation. So it was therefore with great interest that I approached reading Richard Powell’s latest publication, Colorstruck!: Painting, Pigment, Affect (2026). | Lowery Stokes Sims

Just Released: Monoprints by Tala Madani

A new series of unique works on paper is now available from Utopia Editions at David Zwirner. Madani’s first monoprints explore themes of censorship, order, and suspension through the figure of the window washer, which also features in recent paintings by the artist.

  • The Walker Youngbird Foundation names Native artist Dustin Newman the annual recipient of its Núhi grant.
  • A Las Vegas man pleads guilty to a felony violation of the Indian Arts and Crafts Act of 1990 after being charged with selling counterfeit Native American art misrepresented as authentic to consumers.
  • The Drawing Center's Laura Hoptman wins the 2027 Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence, the Joyce Awards winners are announced, Agnes Gund's art nonprofit receives $30 million, Derrick Adams and LEGO make a splash in Miami, and more in Art Movements.

NYSS is now accepting applications from independent thinkers and experimenters in the arts.

Laia Abril Photographs the Instruments of Rape Culture

In her latest show, garments and other objects serve as stand-ins for the systems that allow sexual assault to persist. | Alina Cohen

Her candy-colored drawings lure the eye only to disquiet the mind, exposing the contradictions of so-called clean energy. | Eileen G’Sell

Contemporary Beadworker Ken Williams Jr Awarded Rakow Commission by Corning Museum of Glass

Marking the prize’s 40th year, “I Am the Hungry Cat” is the first Rakow Commission awarded for beadwork.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Most of us remember where we were when we heard that Notre-Dame had burned down. And even upon learning that the most famous of all French cathedrals had been badly damaged rather than completely destroyed, it still felt as if something irreplaceable had been lost. It made no difference whether we’d actually been to the place, as I hadn’t at the time. When I did finally make it to Paris four years later, Notre-Dame’s restoration was still underway, and construction walls prevented anyone from seeing much of anything at ground level, let alone entering. Yet crowds still gathered to take pictures in the square outside, apparently finding that proximity to such a civilizational landmark was enough, even in its partially ruined and inaccessible state.

Even without a chance to step inside, experiencing Notre-Dame’s surroundings on the Île de la Cité, as well as the greater urban context of Paris, certainly deepens one’s understanding of the beauty of the cathedral itself. So does visiting other, less widely known examples of the form, as shown by architecture-and-history YouTuber Manuel Bravo in his new video above.

Ordinary tourists in Paris may make a beeline for Notre-Dame, but they’re hardly likely to find their way out to the other medieval cathedrals in Saint-Denis, north of the city, much less all the way out in Laon. Though glorious in their own way, they’re perhaps even more valuable in providing the context of Gothic church architecture in which Notre-Dame made such a mark.

As Bravo explains it, Notre-Dame’s façade represents “the moment in which Gothic façade achieves its most balanced synthesis. The experiments and innovations of Saint-Denis and Laon are absorbed, disciplined, and unified into a composition in which no element appears arbitrary or independent from the whole.” Among its most influential appreciators was Victor Hugo, in whose time much of Paris’ Gothic architecture was being demolished. His romantic evocations of the medieval built environment in Notre-Dame de Paris (in English, The Hunchback of Notre-Dame) helped save the much deteriorated titular structure, which received an ambitious renovation under Eugène Viollet-le-Duc between 1844 and 1864. That project went beyond period accuracy, adding such non-original details as the gallery of chimeras perched high enough to remain visible during the latest restoration work. Visitors today may notice that the interior doesn’t look exactly like it used to, but some will appreciate that even a monument like Notre-Dame must change with the centuries.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.

Laura Hoptman Wins CCS Bard Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence

The Center for Curatorial Studies at Bard College announced Laura Hoptman, executive director of the Drawing Center in New York, as the recipient of the 2027 Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence, a $25,000 prize. Hoptman's curriculum vitae reads like a roll call of NYC's major institutions: She started out as an assistant curator at the Bronx Museum in the 1980s and later held curatorial roles at the Museum of Modern Art and the New Museum.

So it is no surprise that, when asked what this recognition signified for her, Hoptman chose to invoke the network and community that her career has grown alongside.

“The best kind of professional recognition comes from one's peers, and this is one of the many reasons why this award is so meaningful to me,” Hoptman told Hyperallergic in an email. “It also reminds me how damn lucky I have been to have spent the last 30 years around art and artists in one of the greatest cultural hubs in the world. After all this time, my vocation still fills me with joy.”

items.title: Rare Hilma af Klint Painting Sells for Staggering $12.7M
items.author: Anna Lee
items.summary: The 1920 painting smashed its original sale estimate and the previous benchmark for a work by the Swedish forebearer of abstraction.

images.caption: Lámina de Hyperallergic
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Anna Lee
Rare Hilma af Klint Painting Sells for Staggering $12.7M

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Hilma af Klint's painting “Ser III No. 5” (1920) sold for a record $12.7 million (SEK 128.9 million) at Bukowskis's modern art and design auction in Stockholm today, November 19, fetching over 16 times the upper end of its estimated price.

The first abstract painting by the Swedish artist and "mother of abstraction" to appear on the open market in 30 years, "Ser III No. 5" was one of the 85 geometric paintings the artist produced during a fervent months-long process in 1920. Theosophical symbols, triangles, and circles in "Ser III No. 5" provide insight into af Klint's last engagement with geometric abstraction before she turned to more naturalist watercolors in the last years of her life.

items.title: The Ebullient Ecofeminism of Carolina Caycedo
items.author: Eileen G’Sell
items.summary: Her candy-colored drawings lure the eye only to disquiet the mind, exposing the contradictions of so-called clean energy.

images.caption: Lámina de Hyperallergic
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
The Ebullient Ecofeminism of Carolina Caycedo
The Ebullient Ecofeminism of Carolina Caycedo
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente

items.cleanReaderHtml:
ST LOUIS, MO — A pink lake under an avalanche of digital detritus; a neon rainbow behind a man in a hazmat suit; a gilt sky above a lone wind turbine. These are among the surreal, meticulously rendered scenes in Carolina Caycedo’s series Mineral Intensive (2023–ongoing).

Caycedo’s candy-colored drawings lure the eye only to disquiet the mind, exposing the contradictions of so-called clean energy, whose production often depends on environmentally destructive mineral extraction.

Such visual beguilement — and ecological exigency — anchors Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots, an exhibition of sculpture, video, printmaking, and drawing that explores the joyous, multisensory dimensions of the artist’s activism.

Born and raised in Bogotá, Colombia, the Los Angeles-based artist devoted two years to collaborative research with botanists, plant taxonomists, and Native elders, informing her rendering of prairie and botanical life across the Mississippi River watershed. By turns bright and delicate, Caycedo’s Plant Portraits series (2021–ongoing) lends an ecofeminist bent to the larger show, merging feminine anatomy with botanical illustration.

Like a heavenly necklace, “Celestial Autonomy, the Dance of Big Dipper and North Star” (2023) dangles in the center of the gallery. Constructed of Alaskan nets, buoys, and other fishing equipment — its title honors the indigenous communities in the region.

Across the Mississippi River, another sculptural installation, “Fiesta de la Raíces” (2026), vivifies the National Building Arts Center in Sauget, Illinois. A three-dimensional “portrait” of the area’s root systems, the sculpture resembles a shaggy chandelier of rope, beads, and natural fibers — beckoning admirers to bask in its festive opulence.

At a time when ecological disaster feels ever imminent, art attuned to earthly precarity can often feel didactic or downright drab. Caycedo insists on an alternate vision: Humanity in sync with a resplendent planet — the ground beneath us trembling with riches, the sky adorned with unseen stars.

Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots continues at the Kemper Art Museum at Washington University in St. Louis (One Brookings Drive, St. Louis, Missouri) through January 4, and at the National Building Arts Center (NBAC) (2300 Falling Springs Road, Sauget, Illinois) through December 12. The exhibition was curated by Meredith Malone and James McAnally.

items.title: Harvard Returns Two Skulls Likely Belonging to Enslaved Individuals, More Than 150 Years After They Were Taken From Brazil for Eugenics Studies
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: The remains were welcomed back in solemn ceremonies in Rio de Janeiro and Salvador after years of pressure from researchers, community groups and the Brazilian government. One skull likely belonged to an individual who fought and died in an 1835 slave revolt

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Smart News
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Diplomatic pouch

items.cleanReaderHtml:
More than a century and a half after their remains were removed from Brazil, sent to the United States and used in eugenics studies at Harvard University, the skulls of two people of African descent have finally returned to Brazil.

Last week, the Brazilian government formally repatriated the remains from Harvard’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology , marking the transfer with official ceremonies in the cities of Rio de Janeiro and Salvador , according to a statement . The skulls were carried aboard flights in padded boxes inside reinforced suitcases by Brazilian diplomats, concluding a four-year recovery campaign, the Guardian ’s Tiago Rogero reports.

“The repatriation of human remains represents a fundamental step towards recognizing the memory, history and dignity of the Black population of our country,” Brazil’s minister of human rights and citizenship, Janine Mello, said at the ceremony, according to the Art Newspaper ’s Gabriella Angeleti. “More than a century after they were taken from Brazil, these remains will return to the country to receive the dignified treatment to which they are entitled, in a process built on respect for memory, religious traditions and the communities involved.”

During the trans-Atlantic slave trade , over four million enslaved Africans disembarked in Brazil—more than in any other destination in the Americas. Brazil was the last country in the Western Hemisphere to abolish slavery, in 1888.

Eugenics emerged in the 19th century as the racist, pseudoscientific belief in the selective breeding of human beings. Universities like Harvard at times supported the eugenics movement, with faculty conducting since-discredited research into racial hierarchies. Exploiting enslaved people and their remains under the guise of science was “widespread,” historians Ayah Nuriddin, Graham Mooney and Alexandre I.R. White wrote in a 2020 Lancet article. “American medical education relied on the theft, dissection and display of bodies, many of whom were Black.”

The existence of the two Brazilian skulls at Harvard came to public light in 2022 through a book by historian Christopher D.E. Willoughby and reporting in the student-run Harvard Crimson , which found that the university held remains from at least 19 people likely enslaved in the United States, the Caribbean and Brazil, Rogero reported last year in the Guardian .

While a 2022 university report recommended the repatriation of the remains and Brazilian researchers continued to push for the skulls’ return, negotiations only gained momentum after Brazil’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs joined the talks in late 2024, historian João José Reis told the Guardian last year.

One of the skulls, transferred to the Federal University of Bahia in Salvador, is believed to belong to an enslaved man of Nagô, or Yoruba , origin who fought and died in the January 1835 Malê Revolt , the largest urban slave rebellion in Brazilian history. During that uprising roughly 600 enslaved and freed African Muslims attempted to take control of Salvador before police suppressed the revolt, killing 70 participants. After the man died of his wounds at a Salvador hospital, U.S. diplomat and sugar trader Gideon T. Snow allegedly took his head and shipped it to Boston alongside a note laden with eugenicist beliefs, describing the unnamed man as “one of the chiefs in the affair,” per the Guardian .

Members of the Bahia Islamic Cultural Center in Salvador and the advocacy group Arakunrin campaigned for his return so he could receive a proper burial. “He is our brother and deserves to be buried under Islamic rites,” Sheikh Abdul Hameed Ahmad , the founder of the center, told the Guardian in 2025. Funeral rituals were often denied to enslaved individuals who died in Brazil, per researcher Hannah Romã Bellini Sarno .

Less is known about the second skull, which was entrusted to the National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro. It had been held at the Peabody Museum since 1870, following a transfer from Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology . Museum records indicate that it was obtained by Walter Hunnewell, a Harvard graduate who served as photographer on an 1865-1866 expedition to Brazil led by naturalist Louis Agassiz , with an accompanying note stating the remains had been “exhumed in the streets of Rio de Janeiro,” per the Art Newspaper .

Based on the skull’s size, Harvard researchers suggested it likely belonged to an adult woman. By cross-referencing 19th-century diaries, letters and maps, Bruno Véras , a historian at the University of Toronto Mississauga, concluded the remains may have been taken from Rio’s Cemitério dos Pretos Novos , a burial ground for newly arrived Africans who died during or shortly after arriving in Brazil. “To steal a skull and take it to another country was violent even in the context of racist research,” Veras tells the Guardian .

“This return represents a historical responsibility for the museum,” Juliana Sayão, deputy director of the national museum, said during the Rio ceremony, per the Art Newspaper . “We are confronted with the story of a person whose life was shaped by enslavement and the removal of her body from Brazil. Beyond assuming temporary custody, we are committed to treating this history with respect and responsibility.”

Neither skull will be publicly exhibited or have its image released. Forensic anthropologists at the two Brazilian universities will conduct measurements and microscopic examinations—and, if authorized, genetic or dating analyses—to confirm the individuals’ sex and origins before both are laid to rest with religious rites.

For Brazilian officials, the return marks both a reckoning and a beginning. “This history of slavery cannot be undone,” Irina Feisthauer Silveira, one of the diplomats who escorted the remains back to Brazil, tells the Guardian . “But acknowledging the mistakes of the past with transparency is a first step towards building a more equal, just and less violent future.”

items.title: See the Rare Baby Rhinoceros Born at England's Chester Zoo, an Adorable Boost for Its Vulnerable Species
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: The calf, born October 11, is in good health and exploring a secluded paddock with its mother, out of view of the public

a baby rhino stands in front of a large adult female rhino

items.cleanReaderHtml:
A zoo in England is welcoming an enormous new baby: a greater one-horned rhino. Video footage captured the moment of the calf’s birth at Chester Zoo on October 11, and since then, animal care teams have delighted in watching the baby grow.

“The new calf is gorgeous, big and active,” Emma Evison, team manager for rhinos at Chester Zoo, tells Smithsonian magazine. “Every step of the process so far has been brilliant … and it’s a pleasure to see the calf becoming more confident and curious.”

It will be a few years before the calf gets its namesake horn, but otherwise, newborn greater one-horned rhinos “come out as almost perfect miniatures of their parents,” Evison says. Their skin folds into plates in a way that resembles a coat of armor, and learning how to inhabit their bulky bodies takes some time.

“For the first few days, young rhinos have to work out how their legs are supposed to operate,” she adds. “There’s a bit of wobbliness.”

The baby is healthy, though its sex and weight haven’t yet been announced. Greater one-horned rhino calves are typically around 99 pounds, per a statement from the zoo, and by the time it’s an adult, the animal will be about six feet tall at the shoulder.

The birth marks the fourth calf born to parents Asha and Beni at Chester Zoo. But after siring the calf, Beni died earlier this year from a sudden illness. “It’s lovely to know that his legacy lives on through this calf,” Tom Garland, assistant manager of the rhino team at Chester Zoo, says in the statement. And Asha “has been a brilliant mum to all her youngsters,” he adds. This most recent pregnancy lasted 15 months.

The greater one-horned rhino ’s scientific name is a nod to the animal’s single keratinous protrusion: Rhinoceros unicornis .

Tracking a rhinoceros pregnancy isn’t an easy task. With such thick skin, rhinos are tough targets for ultrasound machines. But caretakers were able to follow Asha’s reproductive cycle by measuring fertility- and pregnancy-related hormones—like estrogen and progesterone—in her dung.

This technique also showed them when Asha was ready to breed, allowing them to safely introduce her to Beni. Rhinos are typically solitary animals outside the mating season, so knowing when they can come together is helpful for zoo scientists hoping to increase their population.

Greater one-horned rhinos once lived throughout the northern region of the Indian subcontinent. But at the start of the 20th century, after widespread habitat loss and relentless hunting driven in part by demand for their horns, only about 200 were left in the wild .

Thanks to decades of conservation efforts and strict protections, the rhinos have come back from the edge of extinction, with some 4,000 of them now living in the wetlands, forests and grasslands of northern India and Nepal.

The species remains vulnerable to extinction, however, and the animals still face risks. Between January 2021 and December 2024, poachers killed nine greater one-horned rhinos in India, and another four were killed in Nepal, Spoorthy Raman reported for Mongabay last year. Many of the wild rhinos are concentrated in only a few national parks, a distribution that “makes them vulnerable to illness and environmental changes,” Mark Brayshaw , the Chester Zoo’s head of mammals, says in the statement. Though the rhinos have more conservation guardrails than they once did, he notes, “they still need people to love and protect them.”

Chester Zoo belongs to a breeding project across Europe that’s working to conserve the rhino species. And this calf is a key part of that effort, since it belongs to a genetically valuable lineage.

“Asha is an important rhino, because her genetic line is not over-represented in this population,” Evison says. Even though her species has seen recent success in the wild, “you don’t know what might happen down the line, so it’s important to have that insurance population of healthy individuals in human care.”

items.cleanReaderHtml:
In the movie The Martian , Matt Damon’s character (botanist Mark Watney) finds himself stranded on Mars. With any rescue months away and food supplies dwindling, he decides to do what he does best—grow some plants. Watley mixes the Martian soil with fertilizer provided by the crew’s waste and plants potatoes.

It’s a good plan (spoiler alert: it worked). Potatoes are both nutritionally dense and provide a high number of calories per unit of land (they’re also versatile and delicious). According to a new study published in npj Microgravity , they may even be able to feed future lunar colonists.

Read more: “ How Potatoes Shaped the Genes of the First People to Grow Them ”

To establish a baseline for best lunar farming practices, a team of botanists from Oregon State University relied on simulated moon soil, or regolith. Unlike the living soil here on Earth, moon dirt isn’t exactly conducive to plant growth—it’s nutrient-poor and contains higher levels of toxic heavy metals. So to give the regolith a little boost, they mixed it with various amounts of vermicompost (an organic fertilizer produced by red wiggler worms) as well as additional nitrogen.

The team tested five varieties of simulated lunar soil, some that mimicked low-lying lunar mares and some that mimicked the highlands. As a control, they used soil from Hermiston, Oregon, which has one of the highest yields of potatoes globally (there goes your reputation, Idaho).

The team found that the optimum mix was 30 percent vermicompost and 70 percent regolith. Potatoes grown in this soil were the best match for those grown in good ol’ Hermiston, Oregon dirt. Lower levels of the fertilizer (5 to 15 percent) yielded stunted tubers, dwarfed leaves, and shriveled roots. (Which region of the moon the regolith simulated—highland versus lowland didn’t seem to make much of a difference.)

Looking at the chemical composition of the potatoes, the researchers found they were nutritionally similar to those grown on Earth. In fact, the vermicompost seems to have provided some protection against heavy metals like copper in the regolith.

“We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter,” study author Aymeric Goyer said in a statement . “That’s an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the Moon.”

Of course, these findings mean future lunar farmers will have to bring vermicompost or something like it to kick-start their agricultural project. But once they get started, they can resupply using their own organic material. After all, as the fictional Mark Watney discovered, astronauts make pretty good fertilizer producers.

items.title: Laia Abril Photographs the Instruments of Rape Culture
items.author: Alina Cohen
items.summary: In her latest show, garments and other objects serve as stand-ins for the systems that allow sexual assault to persist.

images.caption: Lámina de Hyperallergic
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Laia Abril Photographs the Instruments of Rape Culture

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Editor’s Note: The following story contains mentions of sexual assault and harassment. To reach the National Sexual Assault Hotline, call 1-800-656-HOPE (4673) or visit online.rainn.org.

Some institutional rape cases create a glut of content. Recent allegations against Cornell students led to the publication of the accused’s portraits, images of their text messages, and videos of their fraternity house. Tweets and articles flooded the internet, while a journalist’s attempt to identify Jane Doe launched an entire Instagram campaign: Users posted their own pictures with the hashtag #iamjanedoe to help shield the victim. On the other side of the spectrum, reported rapes in the military, the Catholic Church, and less wealthy communities around the world may be met with silence, handled privately, or otherwise fail to galvanize the digital realm. 

Spanish photographer Laia Abril — whose larger project “A History of Misogyny” has also tackled feminicide, abortion, and endometriosis — faces a tricky mandate as she created On Rape and Institutional Failure, first shown in 2020 and now on view at the International Center for Photography. Her images have to be compelling without embracing spectacle, specific while addressing an enormous, global theme.

The artist makes two key choices, one conceptual and one formal: She shoots objects instead of people, all in black-and-white. Honing in on her palette, Abril gets at the seemingly eternal nature of misogyny; her distilled images stoke a similarly condensed rage.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
A forthcoming documentary spotlights the life and work of luminary artist Jean-Michel Basquiat (1960-1988). Directed by Quinn Whitney Wilson and Viridiana Lieberman for Netflix, the feature film is the first project authorized by the artist’s two younger sisters, Lisane Basquiat and Jeanine Heriveaux, who helm his estate.

In a trailer, the siblings describe their brother’s energetic approach to life and how the story typically told about his meteoric rise omits so much of who he really was. Simply titled Jean-Michel Basquiat, the film features archival footage and audio, along with never-before-seen works and commentary from his family. The documentary seeks to venture beyond the mythology that’s come to surround Basquiat, who died of an accidental overdose at just 27 and whose work has continued to captivate the art world.

As one sister says in the trailer, “he was unapologetically Jean-Michel Basquiat.” The documentary will be available for streaming globally on December 11.

items.summary: Subtle shifts in gaze can signal we’re hiding something The post How Our Eyes Betray Us When We Lie appeared first on Nautilus .

items.cleanReaderHtml:
“It takes two to lie: one to lie and one to listen,” isn’t just a famous quote from Homer Simpson, it’s also the spirit of an actual experiment from a new study published in PLOS One . Psychologists from Ulm University in Germany recently investigated how our eyes react when we’re trying to deceive another actual person.

Here’s how they arranged the experiment: We’ll call our protagonist “Participant” and their partner “Mentalist” (because that’s what they called them in the study. During the investigation this pair sat facing one another at a table. Participant first selected a card with a number from one to six (if it’s important to your mental image, they resembled Uno cards). A screen visible to both Participant and Mentalist then showed the cards in sequence for five seconds each. Afterwards, Mentalist got to ask Participant some yes or no questions (i.e., “Is your card even?”) to try to determine which card they picked.

It sounds straightforward, but this is where the lying comes in. Before the sessions, Participant was tasked with either revealing the card to Mentalist, concealing their selection (making sure Mentalist didn’t guess correctly), or faking them out (placing suspicion on another card altogether). Participant was instructed to use nonverbal communication and tailor their question responses to achieve whatever goal they were given. During this little battle of wits, Participant’s eyes were tracked with specialized glasses.

According to data from 36 participants, our eyes betray us. Regardless of whether the participants were trying to reveal, conceal, or fake out the mentalist, their pupils dilated more when their own card popped up on the screen.

Additionally, when participants tried to conceal the identity of their cards, their gazes showed subtle differences. They blinked less and also showed fewer fixations, but for longer durations (0.9 versus 1.2 seconds). The researchers said this was likely a result of arousal inhibition, or a conscious attempt to suppress reactions. Finally, during the verbal portion, the eyes stopped being so instructive. Instead, the response time seemed to give the concealers and fakers away—truthful responses came a full second quicker than lies.

Of course, the study wasn’t designed to determine the effectiveness of the lies, just how people react physiologically when they’re telling them. Still, it seems like meeting someone’s gaze is as effective a tactic as any for sussing out dishonesty.

items.title: Art Dealer Sentenced for Falsely Claiming Native Heritage
items.author: Rhea Nayyar
items.summary: Jose Martinez adopted the name Joseph Skywolf and ran a traveling gallery that sold products falsely marketed as Native, violating the Indian Arts and Crafts Act.

images.caption: Lámina de Hyperallergic
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Rhea Nayyar
Art Dealer Sentenced for Falsely Claiming Native Heritage

items.cleanReaderHtml:
This month, a Las Vegas man pled guilty to a felony violation of the Indian Arts and Crafts Act of 1990 after being charged with selling counterfeit Native American art misrepresented as authentic to consumers. A United States district court judge for Nevada sentenced Jose Martinez, who adopted the name Joseph Skywolf, to two years of supervised probation and court-ordered restitution for the infraction.

A release from the US Department of the Interior's Indian Arts and Crafts Board (IACB) outlined that Martinez falsely claimed to be Chiricahua Apache, Apache, Navajo, and Native American while promoting his mobile business Skywolf's Gallery. Through the business, which was once headquartered in Jackson, Wyoming, but traveled to venues and markets across the Great Plains and Southwest, Martinez deliberately sold counterfeit artwork and handicrafts, including headdresses, jewelry, paintings, and beaded tanned hides falsely attributed to Native artists or specific tribes.

Last summer, Martinez was indicted on one count of violating the Indian Arts and Crafts Act, which prohibits the sale of products falsely marketed as authentic American Indian or Alaska Native art and craftwork. The act is intended to protect the livelihoods, cultural knowledge, and artistic traditions of recognized Native tribes, bands, and communities, as well as consumers seeking authentic cultural heritage and art objects.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Outbreaks caused by falling vaccination rates led to the loss of a public health achievement attained in 2000

US Measles Outbreak and Increase in infection cases concept as a rising deadly outbreak disease and viral illness as a contagious chickenpox or a skin rash.

The United States has lost its measles elimination status – an international designation reflecting an absence of local measles transmission for at least 12 months – a public health achievement held since 2000 . A commission of the Pan American Health Organization, a regional office of the World Health Organization that oversees the Americas, reached that conclusion in November 2026, with a formal announcement expected Nov. 17 .

Canada lost its measles elimination status in 2025 , as did the United Kingdom and other countries in Europe and central Asia in early 2026.

These losses of status are no mystery. Measles is one of the most contagious diseases and still circulates in much of the world . What keeps the disease in check is herd immunity – when a high enough percentage of the population is vaccinated to break the chains of transmission. For measles, that’s at least 95% . But in 2025-26, only 92% of kindergartners in the U.S. received the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine .

I’m an epidemiologist who studies misinformation in the same way others study smoking or air pollution: as an exposure that makes populations sick. For years I’ve watched vaccine misinformation help erode the coverage that kept measles from spreading.

A measles vaccine has existed in the U.S. since 1963 . The combined MMR vaccine followed in 1971; two doses are about 97% effective . A federal program created in 1993 made it free for eligible children . After widespread vaccination efforts, reported cases dropped more than 99% , and by 2000 measles was declared eliminated .

But due to the success of the MMR vaccine, within a generation most parents and many doctors had never even seen a measles case. The experts who certified elimination in 2000 warned that maintaining elimination status would require sustained high rates of vaccination, fast outbreak response and strong surveillance. Drop any one of these conditions and imported cases would spread.

So how does a country with a 97% effective vaccine lose measles elimination status? One obvious explanation: The vaccine worked so well that people forgot what the disease does.

Before the vaccine , measles infected 3 million to 4 million Americans a year. Tens of thousands were hospitalized, and hundreds died. Parents didn’t need convincing. They had seen it. Even with most cases unreported, the official count in 1963 was nearly 400,000 cases .

About 1 in 20 children who contract measles develop pneumonia. The virus can also erase part of the immune system’s memory, an effect called immune amnesia , leaving children open to infections they had already beaten.

In rare cases, it causes a fatal brain disease, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis , which appears years after apparent recovery. In 2025, a child in Los Angeles died of it .

As of Nov. 12, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention counted 5,412 cases for 2026 – the highest number since 1991 – and 591 hospitalizations. Among children under 5, 1 in 6 have been hospitalized .

Six deaths appear in the CDC’s 2026 count, which now relies on federal death certificate data. States, using a broader definition, report a total of 10 deaths: seven in Pennsylvania , one in New York and two in Wisconsin .

items.cleanReaderHtml:
The first time I encountered Yoshitomo Nara’s work was when I opened the mailbox as an angsty teenager. A friend a few years older had recently visited the Walker Art Center, where she bought a postcard printed with two of the artist’s portraits and scribbled a note to her friend (me) still stuck in their tiny Wisconsin hometown. As is wont to happen to teenagers on the cusp of adulthood, I took that postcard as a sort of guiding light—a reminder that the world was bigger than the tractors and small-town gossip I was surrounded by—and promptly cut and taped the works to fit within my clear phone case. I carried this pair of strange characters everywhere I went for years after.

Nara also was born and raised in a rural region, albeit on the other side of the globe. The artist has described his childhood in Aomori on the northern tip of Japan’s main island as solitary and removed from the culture of the cities, instead flanked by the endless expanse of the Pacific Ocean and the snowy ridges of the Hakkōda Mountains. These early years indelibly informed his sensibility, and even in his most emotionally charged works, there’s a deep sense of calm that comes from immersion in nature.

In his first solo presentation in New York in almost a decade, Nara takes over two of David Zwirner’s galleries. The self-titled exhibition includes nearly 100 works from the last several decades, spanning paintings, drawings, and monumental bronze sculptures. Central are the artist’s signature childlike figures with large heads and eyes and an underlying sense of innocence, their skeptical, bored, and even rebellious expressions providing a necessary counterbalance—one that also spoke to my teenage sensitivities.

Profoundly enigmatic, Nara’s works are also instantly recognizable, relatable, and broadly appealing. According to the gallery, 4,000 visitors lined up to see the exhibition on opening night, with 26,000 attending in the first week alone.

Ranging in scale from intimate miniatures to larger-than-life, Nara’s two-dimensional portraits emerge from soft, pastel-hued palettes. Several also often contain pithy phrases that hearken to our collective challenges. Both “world peace” and “tomorrow’s far away” drip with longing and speak to the artist’s broader concern for the contentious state of human relations.

Introducing clay into his practice also emerged from unease and grief, when Nara picked up the earthen material after the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake. The disastrous event killed nearly 20,000 people and injured and displaced many more around the artist’s hometown. In the moment, the tactile medium offered a reprieve the canvas couldn’t.

In the exhibition, Nara’s monochromatic bronzes, coated in white urethane paint, capture these forays into three-dimensions and evoke the icy, snow-blanketed landscapes of his youth. Based on smaller ceramic prototypes, the sculptures bear the traces of the handmade, as if he had sculpted each head with an enormous thumb.

As an exhibition statement says, Nara’s overarching impulse is simple: he “creates art in order to express and communicate what he feels unable to convey in words, and his distinctive body of work has evolved through his ongoing search to identify what is uniquely his: his upbringing in rural northern Japan at a particular moment in time and, above all, his profound concern for humanity, including those outside mainstream society.”

The artist recently wrapped up a large-scale project at the Hirshorn Sculpture Garden, and next fall, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art will host a major retrospective of his work. Until then, see Yoshitomo Nara through December 12 in New York.
